paper_a.title: An Elementary Proof of a Theorem of Johnson and Lindenstrauss

paper_b.title: Database-friendly Random Projections: Johnson-Lindenstrauss with Binary Coins

metadata.description: Both papers re-derive the Johnson-Lindenstrauss dimension-reduction guarantee via an elementary chain of MGF / Markov arguments. Dasgupta-Gupta use a Gaussian random projection (uniform random k-dimensional subspace, equivalently i.i.d. N(0,1) entries); Achlioptas replaces the Gaussian entries with i.i.d. Rademacher +/-1 (or sparse +/-sqrt(3),0) coins and recovers the same k = O(log n / epsilon^2) bound. The shared backbone is: per-vector concentration of |f(alpha)|^2 around its mean k/d via an MGF + Markov + parameter-optimisation, then a union bound over n^2 pairs. Paper105 (Dasgupta-Gupta) explicitly cites Achlioptas in its closing remark, confirming a parallel-rediscovery / variant relationship rather than a hierarchical extension. Both inputs are PDF-fallback extractions, so confidences for math-heavy matches are dropped one notch.

matches.explanation: Both are the main JL guarantee of the paper: for any n points in R^d, a randomly drawn map f : R^d -> R^k with k >= C(epsilon^2/2 - epsilon^3/3)^{-1} log n preserves all pairwise squared distances within (1 +/- epsilon). The leading constant differs (Dasgupta-Gupta: 4; Achlioptas: 4 + 2 beta with success prob 1 - n^{-beta}), and the random map differs (Gaussian subspace vs. +/-1 / sparse-sign matrix), but the theorem statement is identical. PDF-fallback fidelity is reduced; names, k-form, and the (1 +/- epsilon) bound match transparently, so we keep the match exact and tag confidence high.
Both are the original 1984 JL Lemma cited from Johnson and Lindenstrauss; same statement (k = O(epsilon^{-2} log n) suffices), both flagged origin: external with the same citation.

LP105.1 is the per-vector concentration: the squared projected length L = ||Z||^2 of a uniformly random unit vector concentrates around its mean k/d with sub-exponential tails of the form exp(-(k/2)(1 - beta + ln beta)). Achlioptas's LP106.2 is the Gaussian-entry version of the same concentration (matching LP105.1 directly: both use i.i.d. N(0,1) entries) and LP106.3 is the discrete-coin version. Together they cover the same role LP105.1 plays in Dasgupta-Gupta. Match is analogous because the parametrisation differs (Achlioptas presents both tails with the (epsilon^2/2 - epsilon^3/3) form already simplified, whereas Dasgupta-Gupta keep the raw beta form) and because LP106.3 is over discrete distributions, not the Gaussian sphere.

Both clusters define the random-projection construction. Dasgupta-Gupta build a uniform unit vector via Gaussian normalisation (DP105.1) and let L = ||Z||^2 be its squared first-k-coordinates norm with mean k/d (DP105.2). Achlioptas defines the d x k random sign matrix R (DP106.2) and the embedding f via E = (1/sqrt(k)) A R (DP106.3). Same mathematical role -- a randomly drawn linear map whose squared output norm concentrates around the input norm -- but the random object (uniform on S^{d-1} vs. discrete-sign matrix) is different by design; that difference IS the contribution of Achlioptas, hence analogous rather than exact.

DP106.1 is the abstract definition of a JL-embedding (a map f preserving squared distances within (1 +/- epsilon)); EP106.1 records the unbiasedness E[||f(alpha)||^2] = ||alpha||^2 (analog of E[L] = k/d up to the (1/sqrt(k)) rescaling). Together they play the same role as DP105.2 in Dasgupta-Gupta: identifying the random projected length and its mean as the central object.

EP105.2 is the Gaussian MGF E[e^{sX^2}] = 1/sqrt(1 - 2s); LP106.4 is the analogous MGF moment bound E[exp(h Q_1^2)] <= 1/sqrt(1 - 2h/d) plus E[Q_1^4] <= 3/d^2 for Achlioptas's discrete entries. Both are the workhorse exponential-moment input fed into the Markov-Chernoff bound; Achlioptas's bound is wider (it must hold for the discrete case) but matches the Gaussian formula's shape exactly -- this is precisely the moment-domination identity that makes the discrete proof work.

Both are the Chernoff-style optimisation step: choose the MGF parameter to minimise the bound. Dasgupta-Gupta give the closed-form optimum t_0 = (1 - beta)/(2 beta (d - k beta)); Achlioptas's PSP106.4 sets the analogous derivative to zero, obtaining h = (d/2) epsilon/(1+epsilon). Cross-type match (equation node vs. proof_step) -- justified because in both papers this is the single step that pins down the bound. Confidence medium because PDF-fallback obscures whether the optimal-parameter algebra is identical line-by-line.

EP105.4 records the log inequalities ln(1-x) <= -x - x^2/2 and ln(1+x) <= x - x^2/2 + x^3/3, used to convert the raw Chernoff exponent into the (epsilon^2/2 - epsilon^3/3)/2 form. PSP106.4 performs the same series expansion to reach exp(-k(epsilon^2/2 - epsilon^3/3)/2). Different node types and granularity (an equation vs. a proof step), but the same purpose -- elementary log/exp series bounding to recover the canonical JL constant.

PP105.1 is the (high-level) proof of the main JL theorem in Dasgupta-Gupta: project to a random k-subspace, use Lemma 2.2 to bound per-pair distortion, union bound. Achlioptas does not have a separate proof node for TP106.1; the union-bound / per-pair argument lives in EP106.2 (the JL probability-target inequality combining concentration + union bound), with the per-vector concentration drawn from LP106.3. Together LP106.3 + EP106.2 reconstitute the same proof structure as PP105.1.

Both papers prove their per-vector concentration lemma by the same recipe: write Pr[...] = Pr[exp(t * stuff) >= 1], apply Markov, factor the MGF over independent coordinates / columns, plug in the Gaussian (resp. discrete) MGF bound, then optimise the free parameter. PP105.2 and PP105.3 cover the lower- and upper-tail halves of the Dasgupta-Gupta lemma; PP106.1 covers both tails of Achlioptas's discrete lemma. Given the same Markov+MGF+optimise template, this is the same proof modulo entry distribution -- the additional moment-domination machinery (LP106.5-7 / PP106.3-5) is precisely what Achlioptas needs to reduce his discrete MGF to the Gaussian one used by Dasgupta-Gupta.

Composite L2-vs-L2 entry under the matched parents (PP105.2/3 ↔ PP106.1). The two step DAGs run almost step-for-step parallel: (a) Markov on the MGF (PSP105.5 ↔ PSP106.1), (b) factor over independence to get a product of one-coordinate MGFs (PSP105.6 ↔ PSP106.2), (c) substitute the Gaussian (resp. discrete) MGF closed form (implicit in PSP105.6 ↔ PSP106.3), (d) optimise the parameter to obtain the Chernoff exponent (PSP105.7 ↔ PSP106.4), (e) handle the lower tail symmetrically (PP105.3 ↔ PSP106.5). The Achlioptas decomposition is finer because its proof must also expand exp(-h Q^2) for the lower tail, but the macroscopic correspondence is tight.

Composite L2-vs-L1 entry (per v2 rule 2): Achlioptas does not unfold the union-bound proof of TP106.1 into proof_step nodes; that whole substructure is captured by EP106.2 (per-vector concentration combined with union bound over pairs implies the JL guarantee). Dasgupta-Gupta's PP105.1 IS unfolded -- setup (PSP105.1), lower-tail bound (PSP105.2), upper-tail bound (PSP105.3), union-bound + rescaling + boost (PSP105.4) -- so we group all four child steps to the single EP106.2 node. Justified in explanation per v2 §Level-2 rule 2.

RP105.1 is the closing remark in Dasgupta-Gupta that explicitly cites Indyk-Motwani and Achlioptas, noting that Achlioptas's +/-1 entries recover the same k bound as their Gaussian proof. This remark is paper105-specific and itself constitutes the strongest pair-level evidence for relation_type = PR. (Auxiliary node, but kept here because it is load-bearing for the relation classification.)

EP105.1 is the equivalent algebraic restatement of Lemma 2.2(a) used internally by Dasgupta-Gupta's MGF derivation. Achlioptas's proof structures the same content differently (via Lemma 6 / LP106.4) and does not surface a corresponding restatement equation, so no counterpart is emitted.

DP106.4 defines the all-ones unit vector w = (1/sqrt(d))(1,...,1) as the worst-case input. This concept is specific to Achlioptas: it underlies the moment-domination chain (LP106.5: w maximises even moments) needed because the entries are discrete and not rotationally symmetric. Dasgupta-Gupta's Gaussian projection is rotation-invariant, so the worst-case-vector reduction is unnecessary on their side.

LP106.5 (Lemma 7: even moments are maximised at w) is a paper106-specific contribution. With Gaussian entries this lemma is trivial by rotation-invariance, so Dasgupta-Gupta have no analogue. Together with LP106.6 / LP106.7 it is the heart of Achlioptas's reduction from discrete coins to the Gaussian MGF bound.

LP106.6 (Lemma 8: even moments of Q(w) dominated by those of N(0, 1/d)) is the second link in Achlioptas's discrete-to-Gaussian moment-domination chain. Has no counterpart in Dasgupta-Gupta because their entries are already Gaussian.
LP106.7 (Lemma 9: pairwise moment-swap inequality) -- the technical core of Achlioptas's Lemma 7 proof. Specific to discrete entries; no Dasgupta-Gupta analogue.

AP106.1 is the database-friendly random-projection algorithm: sample R with discrete-sign entries, compute E = (1/sqrt(k)) A R via simple aggregations, optionally drop 2/3 of attributes (sparse case). This algorithm-as-a-first-class-object is the headline contribution of Achlioptas; Dasgupta-Gupta describe their projection only as 'pick a random k-subspace' inside the proof and do not have an algorithm node.
Proof of LP106.5 -- support machinery for Achlioptas's discrete-to-Gaussian reduction. No Dasgupta-Gupta counterpart.
Proof of LP106.6 -- support machinery for Achlioptas's discrete-to-Gaussian reduction. No Dasgupta-Gupta counterpart.
Proof of LP106.7 (the binomial-expansion / D_{2j} >= 0 argument for the pairwise moment swap). Specific to Achlioptas; no Dasgupta-Gupta analogue.
